Turkey Imposes Temporary Seafood Export Ban, Rocking Fisheries Sector

A temporary government ban on seafood exports, announced last week, has sent shockwaves through Turkey’s fisheries industry, leaving many firms, processing sites, and workers in a state of uncertainty. The measure, introduced by the Ministry of Trade in an effort to stabilize domestic supply and address recent price surges, prohibits the export of all major fish products, including anchovy, sea bass, and trout.

The embargo, effective immediately and set for an initial period of three months, has already caused disruptions at processing plants and aquaculture farms across the Black Sea and Aegean coasts. "We have hundreds of tonnes of fish ready for shipment that are now stuck in cold storage," said Ahmet Acar, general manager at Karadeniz Balikçılık, a mid-sized fisheries firm in Trabzon. "Our international contracts are on hold, and we’re facing mounting storage costs by the day."

The ban directly impacts tens of thousands of workers employed in harvesting, processing, and packaging. Local union leaders report rising anxiety among seasonal staff. “Many workers rely on peak export periods for their annual income,” said Derya Demir, spokesperson for the National Fisheries Workers Union. “This sudden halt has left families uncertain about their paychecks.”

Industry analysts estimate that Turkish seafood exporters stand to lose up to 40% of their quarterly revenue if the embargo remains in place. The Aegean Fisheries Producers Association has appealed for government support, warning that smaller firms may face closures if relief is not provided. “We understand the goal of keeping fish affordable at home, but the livelihoods of our communities are at stake,” said association head Murat Can.

Firms are now shifting focus to the domestic market, but many say local demand cannot absorb the entire surplus. As the embargo continues, stakeholders are urging officials to consider targeted measures instead of a blanket ban. The Ministry of Trade has stated it will review the policy’s impact before the end of the embargo period.
